notes.definition: Metals are good conductors of electricity because their delocalised electrons can move through the structure and carry electrical charge. Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred through the metal by the delocalised electrons.
explanation: In a metal, the outer shell electrons of the metal atoms are delocalised. This means they are not tied to any one atom but are free to move throughout the whole giant structure, while the positive metal ions stay in fixed positions in the lattice. These delocalised electrons are the key to explaining why metals are such good conductors.

An electric current is a flow of charge. When a potential difference is applied across a metal, for example by connecting a wire to a cell, the delocalised electrons, which are negatively charged, move through the metal towards the positive terminal. So the delocalised electrons carry electrical charge through the metal. This happens in the solid state; a metal does not need to be melted or dissolved to conduct. The positive ions do not move through the metal.

Metals are also good conductors of thermal energy (heat). When one part of a metal is heated, the delocalised electrons there gain energy. Because they are free to move through the structure, they quickly transfer this energy to other parts of the metal. This is why the handle of a metal spoon gets hot when it is left in a hot drink.

Compare metals with other types of substance. Ionic compounds do not conduct when solid because their ions are held in fixed positions; they conduct only when melted or dissolved, when the ions can move. Simple molecular substances and most giant covalent substances, such as diamond, have no delocalised electrons or ions, so they do not conduct electricity. Graphite is an exception: like a metal, it has delocalised electrons and so conducts electricity.

These properties explain many uses of metals. Copper is used for electrical wiring because it is an excellent electrical conductor and can be drawn into wires. Aluminium and stainless steel are used for saucepans because they conduct thermal energy well, transferring energy from the hob to the food. Handles are often made from plastic or wood, which are poor conductors, so they stay cool.
keyFacts: Metals contain delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure.
Metals are good conductors of electricity because delocalised electrons carry electrical charge through the metal.
Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.
Metals conduct electricity when solid and when liquid.
The positive metal ions stay in fixed positions; it is the electrons that move.
Ionic solids do not conduct because their ions cannot move; molten or dissolved ionic compounds do conduct.
Graphite is a non-metal that conducts because it also has delocalised electrons.
Copper is used for electrical wires; metals such as aluminium are used for saucepans.

keyTerms.definition: Electrons that are not attached to a particular atom and are free to move throughout a structure.
A material that allows electric charge to flow through it.
A material that transfers thermal energy (heat) through it quickly.
A flow of electrical charge. In a metal, the charge is carried by delocalised electrons.
A material that does not conduct electricity (or thermal energy) well, such as plastic.

workedExamples.title: Explaining electrical conductivity
workedExamples.question: Explain why copper conducts electricity.
steps: Identify the structure: copper is a metal with a giant structure of positive ions.
Identify the mobile particles: the outer electrons are delocalised.
Say what they do: the delocalised electrons can move through the structure.
Link to conduction: they carry electrical charge through the metal.
workedExamples.answer: Copper has delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure and carry electrical charge.

workedExamples.title: Comparing a metal and an ionic compound
workedExamples.question: Solid magnesium conducts electricity but solid magnesium oxide does not. Explain why.
steps: Magnesium is a metal: it has delocalised electrons that can move and carry charge.
Magnesium oxide is ionic: it contains charged ions, but in the solid they are held in fixed positions in the lattice.
Because neither the ions nor any electrons can move through solid magnesium oxide, no charge can flow.
workedExamples.answer: Magnesium has delocalised electrons that move and carry charge. In solid magnesium oxide the ions cannot move and there are no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals conduct electricity because the positive ions move.
misconceptions.right: In fact the positive ions stay in fixed positions in the lattice. The delocalised electrons move and carry the charge.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think metals must be melted to conduct electricity, as ionic compounds must.
misconceptions.right: In fact metals conduct when solid because their delocalised electrons are already free to move.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that metals conduct because they have 'free ions' or 'free electrons in shells'.
misconceptions.right: In fact the correct phrase is 'delocalised electrons' that are free to move through the whole structure.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think only metals conduct electricity.
misconceptions.right: In fact graphite, a non-metal, also conducts because it has delocalised electrons, and molten or dissolved ionic compounds conduct because their ions can move.

realWorld: Copper is used for electrical wiring in homes because it is an excellent conductor of electricity.
Saucepans are made of metals such as aluminium or stainless steel because they conduct thermal energy from the hob to the food quickly.
Metal heat sinks in computers conduct thermal energy away from the processor to stop it overheating.
examTips: Always say 'delocalised electrons' and include what they do: 'carry charge' for electricity and 'transfer energy' for thermal conduction.
Never say ions move in a metal; this contradicts a correct answer and can lose the mark.
When comparing conductivity of different substances, say what the charged particles are and whether they can move.
Learn graphite as the non-metal exception: it conducts because it has delocalised electrons, just like metals.
summary: Metals have delocalised electrons that are free to move.
Delocalised electrons carry electrical charge, so metals conduct electricity.
Delocalised electrons transfer energy, so metals conduct thermal energy.
Metals conduct when solid; the positive ions do not move.
Ionic solids do not conduct because their ions are fixed.
Graphite also conducts because it has delocalised electrons.

flashcards.front: Which particles carry charge in a metal?
Do the positive ions move when a metal conducts?

flashcards.front: Do metals need to be melted to conduct?
flashcards.back: No. Solid metals conduct because their delocalised electrons are free to move.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't solid sodium chloride conduct?

flashcards.front: When does an ionic compound conduct?
flashcards.back: When melted or dissolved in water, because the ions can then move.

flashcards.front: Which non-metal conducts electricity like a metal?

questions.question: Which particles allow metals to conduct electricity?
markScheme: 1 mark: Delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge. Positive ions stay fixed, and protons and neutrons are in the nuclei.

questions.question: Why are metals good conductors of thermal energy?
options: Their positive ions move from the hot end to the cold end
Energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: Energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons gain energy and move through the metal, transferring energy to cooler parts.

questions.question: Which metal is most commonly used for electrical wiring in homes?
markScheme: 1 mark: Copper
questions.explanation: Copper is an excellent electrical conductor, can be drawn into wires and is much cheaper than gold.

questions.question: In which state does a metal conduct electricity?
markScheme: 1 mark: When solid and when liquid
questions.explanation: Metals have delocalised electrons in both the solid and liquid states, so they conduct in both. It is ionic compounds that need to be molten or dissolved.

questions.question: What happens to the positive metal ions when an electric current flows through a copper wire?
options: They move towards the negative terminal
They move towards the positive terminal
They stay in fixed positions in the lattice
markScheme: 1 mark: They stay in fixed positions in the lattice
questions.explanation: The positive ions vibrate about fixed positions. Only the delocalised electrons flow through the wire.

questions.question: Which substance conducts electricity when solid?
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium is a metal with delocalised electrons. Sodium chloride's ions are fixed in the solid, and sulfur and silicon dioxide have no free charged particles.

questions.question: Which statement about electrical conduction is correct?
options: Solid ionic compounds conduct because they contain ions
Metals conduct because their delocalised electrons carry charge
Simple molecular substances conduct when solid
Metals conduct because their ions are free to move
markScheme: 1 mark: Metals conduct because their delocalised electrons carry charge
questions.explanation: Only metals (and graphite) have delocalised electrons. Ionic solids contain ions but they cannot move, so they do not conduct.

questions.question: Which non-metal conducts electricity for a similar reason to metals?
markScheme: 1 mark: Graphite
questions.explanation: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom, so like a metal it has electrons free to move and carry charge.

questions.question: A substance does not conduct electricity when solid, but does when molten. It does not contain delocalised electrons. Which type of substance is it most likely to be?
markScheme: 1 mark: An ionic compound
questions.explanation: Metals and graphite conduct when solid. Ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved, because then their ions can move.

questions.question: A student says: 'Metals conduct electricity because their electrons are free to move between the shells of each atom.' What is the best correction?
options: The electrons are free to move through the whole structure, not just within one atom
The ions, not the electrons, are free to move
Metals conduct because their nuclei are charged
markScheme: 1 mark: The electrons are free to move through the whole structure, not just within one atom
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons are not tied to any particular atom; they can move through the whole metal structure, which is what allows charge to flow.

questions.question: Why is a metal saucepan often given a plastic handle?
options: Plastic is a poor conductor of thermal energy, so the handle stays cool
Plastic conducts thermal energy better than metal
Plastic makes the saucepan heat up faster
markScheme: 1 mark: Plastic is a poor conductor of thermal energy, so the handle stays cool
questions.explanation: Metals conduct thermal energy well, so a metal handle would get hot. Plastic is a poor thermal conductor (an insulator).

questions.question: Name the particles that carry electrical charge through a metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: (delocalised) electrons
questions.explanation: In metals, the charge carriers are the delocalised electrons.

questions.question: State one property of metals that makes copper suitable for electrical wires.
markScheme: 1 mark: good conductor of electricity / can be bent or drawn into wires
questions.explanation: Copper's delocalised electrons make it an excellent electrical conductor, and its layers can slide so it can be drawn into wires.

questions.question: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity.
markScheme: 1 mark: metals have delocalised electrons
1 mark: which are free to move through the structure and carry (electrical) charge
questions.explanation: Both points are needed: the delocalised electrons and the idea that they move and carry charge.

questions.question: Explain why metals are good conductors of thermal energy.
markScheme: 1 mark: delocalised electrons (gain energy and) move through the metal
1 mark: transfer energy (to cooler parts)
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons are free to move, so they can carry energy from hotter to cooler parts of the metal.

questions.question: Explain why solid potassium chloride does not conduct electricity, but solid potassium does.
markScheme: 1 mark: in solid potassium chloride the ions are in fixed positions and cannot move (no delocalised electrons)
1 mark: potassium is a metal with delocalised electrons that can move and carry charge
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. Potassium has them (delocalised electrons); solid potassium chloride does not, because its ions are locked in the lattice.

questions.question: In which direction do the delocalised electrons move in a metal wire connected to a cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: towards the positive terminal
questions.explanation: Electrons are negatively charged, so they are attracted towards the positive terminal.

questions.question: Suggest why aluminium is used to make saucepans and why the handles are often made of plastic.
markScheme: 1 mark: aluminium is a good thermal conductor (delocalised electrons transfer energy to the food)
1 mark: plastic is a poor thermal conductor so the handle does not get hot
questions.explanation: Use the contrast: metal conducts energy to the food quickly, while plastic insulates the hand.

questions.question: Graphite and copper both conduct electricity. Identify the feature their structures have in common and explain how it allows conduction.
markScheme: 1 mark: both have delocalised electrons
1 mark: which are free to move through the structure and carry charge
questions.explanation: Graphite is similar to metals because it has delocalised electrons, one from each carbon atom.

questions.question:
A student tests four solids, A to D, for electrical conductivity.
A: conducts; melting point 1085 °C
B: does not conduct; melting point 801 °C; conducts when molten
C: does not conduct; melting point 114 °C; does not conduct when molten
D: conducts; melting point 98 °C
Identify which solids are metals and explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: A and D are metals
1 mark: they conduct when solid because they have delocalised electrons that can move and carry charge
1 mark: B does not conduct when solid but does when molten so is ionic (ions can only move when molten) / C never conducts so has no free charged particles
questions.explanation: Only metals (and graphite) conduct as solids. A low melting point (D, which matches sodium) does not rule out a metal: conductivity is the deciding test.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a metal and explain why metals conduct electricity and thermal energy.
markScheme: Indicative content: giant structure / lattice; positive metal ions in regular layers; outer electrons are delocalised; delocalised electrons free to move through the whole structure; metallic bonding is the attraction between ions and delocalised electrons; electricity: delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal (towards the positive terminal); ions stay in fixed positions; thermal energy: delocalised electrons gain energy and transfer it through the metal to cooler regions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the structure including delocalised electrons, with correct explanations of both electrical and thermal conduction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): mentions electrons or delocalised electrons but explains only one type of conduction, or the explanation is unclear (for example, says ions move).
questions.explanation: Answers must cover both properties, each linked to the delocalised electrons.

questions.question:
Electrical cables have a copper core surrounded by a layer of poly(ethene) or PVC.
Explain why copper and a polymer are used for these parts of the cable. Use ideas about structure and bonding in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: copper is a metal with a giant structure of positive ions; outer electrons are delocalised; delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure; they carry electrical charge, so copper is a good conductor and allows current to flow; positive ions stay in fixed positions; copper layers can slide so it can be drawn into wires and bent. The polymer is made of very large molecules; atoms joined by covalent bonds; all outer electrons are held in covalent bonds; there are no delocalised electrons and no ions; so there are no charged particles free to move; the polymer does not conduct electricity (insulator); prevents electric shocks and short circuits; it is also flexible and solid at room temperature because of relatively strong intermolecular forces.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, coherent explanation of why copper conducts and why the polymer does not, both clearly linked to structure and bonding and to the function of each part of the cable.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains why copper conducts with reference to delocalised electrons and gives some reason why the polymer does not conduct, with limited structural detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'copper conducts and plastic does not', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The best answers contrast the delocalised electrons in copper with the absence of any mobile charged particles in the covalently bonded polymer.

questions.question: Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature. Predict whether liquid mercury conducts electricity and explain your prediction.
acceptedAnswers: still free to move in liquid
markScheme: 1 mark: yes, it conducts
1 mark: it is a metal, so it still has delocalised electrons that can move and carry charge
questions.explanation: Metals conduct in both the solid and liquid states because their delocalised electrons are present in both.

questions.question: Compare how electrical charge is carried in a copper wire and in molten sodium chloride.
markScheme: Indicative content: copper: metal; delocalised electrons; free to move through the structure; carry charge; positive ions stay fixed; conducts when solid and liquid. Molten sodium chloride: ionic compound; contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; in the molten state the ions are free to move; ions carry the charge; in the solid the ions are fixed so it does not conduct; no delocalised electrons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison identifying the different charge carriers (electrons versus ions) and when each can move.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies one charge carrier correctly, or states both conduct without explaining how.
questions.explanation: A comparison should name the charge carrier in each case (delocalised electrons in copper, moving ions in molten sodium chloride) and explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct.

questions.question: When one end of a copper rod is heated, the other end soon becomes hot. What is the main way energy is transferred along the rod?
options: Copper ions move from the hot end to the cold end
Delocalised electrons gain energy and move through the metal, transferring it
Air inside the metal carries the energy
Covalent bonds between copper atoms break and re-form
markScheme: 1 mark: Delocalised electrons gain energy and move through the metal, transferring it
questions.explanation: In metals, delocalised electrons transfer energy quickly through the structure. The ions stay in place and copper has metallic, not covalent, bonding.

questions.question: State why sulfur, a simple molecular solid, does not conduct electricity.
acceptedAnswers: no charged particles free to move
markScheme: 1 mark: it has no delocalised electrons or ions (no charged particles free to move)
questions.explanation: Simple molecular substances have all their outer electrons in covalent bonds and no ions, so nothing can carry charge.
